newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian cocoa arrivals nudge 820,000 T by Feb 10.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian cocoa arrivals nudge 820,000 T by Feb 10.

text.p: Cocoa arrivals at Ivorian ports ranged from 810,000 to 820,000 tonnes by February 10 against 880,000 tonnes in the record 1995/96 season, industry sources say.
One Abidjan-based exporter predicted a slowdown in main crop (Oct-March) volumes before midcrop arrivals (April-Sept).
Arrivals figures compiled by February 7 suggested a cumulative total since October 1 of 550,000 tonnes of cocoa taken to Abidjan and another 250,000 tonnes to San Pedro.
Sources said another 20,000 tonnes of cocoa had arrived by Monday after formal arrivals figures had been compiled.
One source put arrivals by Wednesday at close to 840,000 tonnes.

Quality inspectors said bean humidity levels this week averaged 7.5-8 percent with bean sizes of 95-100 per 100 grammes. Both figures are within respective export standards of eight percent and 105 beans per 100 grammes.
Ivory Coast produced a record 1.2 million tonne crop in 1995/96 after a larger than expected 200,000 tonnes mid crop.
It has forecast a total 1996/97 crop of 950,000 tonnes but some private forecasters expect over a million tonnes.

Weather patterns up to the end of February would determine midcrop flower survival and pod setting rates, local crop analysts said. Weather data showed light rains in mainly southern areas in the second ten days of January.
One crop analyst told Reuters a crop of 1.1 million tonnes would be possible if favourable weather with 10 mm a week prevailed in February. Exporters expect less.
Latest official weather data is still being compiled.

Ivory Coast's warehouses remain full to a capacity of up to 400,000 tonnes. One London trader said the strength of sterling, a principal cocoa trading currency, encouraged hedging with Ivorian cocoa and had discouraged industry buying.
Stocks rose in January on low world prices and demand.
Exports in 1996/97 continue to lag well behind arrivals, with 416,000 tonnes shipped by the end of January.
"Exporters have slowed down buying," said one forwarder. "We will probably see a tail-off in about eight days and a calmer period before the midcrop kicks in," he added.

One ship for Philadelphia was loading 7,000 tonnes of pre-slung palleted cocoa at Abidjan on Wednesday. Another 3,000 tonnes of mega-bulk was loaded at the weekend with a further 5,000 tonnes shipped in palleted jute bags.
Exporters and forwarders expect large shipments to leave against March contracts before midcrop port arrivals begin.
In 1995/96 some exporters overdeclared arrivals early in the season to attract finance while underdeclaring later to balance their year's account.
